text: 82.1 Deployment Scenarios

* 9 The indoor picocell is the targeted deployment scenario of this specification. The requirements of the indoor 10 picocell base station are listed in the white box Deployment Scenarios and Base Station Classes document 11 \[1\]. Some of the key requirements described in that document are highlighted here.
  * 12 Cell type: Indoor
  * 13 Carrier Frequency Band: FR1
  * 14 Frequency Bandwidth: Up to 100 MHz

182.2 White Box Base Station Architecture

* 19 In general, the base station hardware architecture can be classified by using different criteria. The physical 20 partition method is adopted by O-RAN; hence, the base station architecture is divided into three categories 21 namely split, integrated, and all-in-one. In split architecture, the fronthaul interface determines the gNB 22 functions location. Here we refer to the two partitions as O-DUx and O-RUx; where the "x" is split option 23 number. In case the O-RAN WG4 defined fronthaul interface is used, these two partitions are called O-DU7-2 24 and O-RU7-2. For a more complete description of the terminology used, refer to the Deployment Scenarios and 25 Base Station Classes Document \[1\].
  * 26 The split architecture is shown in Figure 2-1. A Fronthaul Gateway \(FHGW\) is an optional device between the 27 O-DUx and O-RUx to aggregate multiple radio units together. Within this specification, a Back End fronthaul 28 interface is defined as the connection between the FHGWx and the O-DUx, while the Font End fronthaul 29 interface is defined as the connection between the FHGWx and the O-RUx. With split architectures, one may 30 choose to have O-CU and O-DUx as either co-located or shared configuration with respect to hardware.
32 Figure 2-1: Indoor Split Architecture
For integrated base station architecture, the O-DU is integrated with the O-RU into one box. Figure 2-2 shows the integrated architecture.

2.2.1 Split RAN Architecture
trace: 182.2 White Box Base Station Architecture --> 2.2.1 Split RAN Architecture

text: For medium and large coverage indoor deployment scenarios, the base station with split RAN architecture is more cost effective. This type of architecture is widely deployed in 4G networks. The main idea of this architecture is "shared cell". By using the fronthaul gateway, a large number of radio units can then share the same radio spectrum resource in one cell. This configuration is very useful in both low and high capacity scenarios. Therefore, when an O-DU\_x and FHGW\_x are capable of handling cell splits, multiple O-RU\_x\(s\) can be grouped together to share the radio resources. Accordingly, the choice of fronthaul split option changes the architecture of the base station. WG7 has recognized the following four split option architectures per service providers' deployment needs which are shown in Figure 2-4 through Figure 2-7.

84.6 FHGWx – Common Requirements

* 9 A Fronthaul gateway is used in many scenarios as the aggregation point of radio units, as well as to provide
  * 10 power to the O-RUs. The FHGWx usually is deployed close to O-RUs \(e.g. indoor coverage: deployed on the
  * 11 same floor or in the same building with multiple radios less than 100 meters\). FHGWx distributes traffic
  * 12 from the O-DUx to each O-RUx, and it combines the uplink traffic from all radios before sending it to the O-
  * 13 DUx. The benefit of using the FHGWx includes radio traffic aggregation and centralized power supplied to
  * 14 radio units. When different fronthaul interfaces are used by the O-DUx and O-RUx, the FHGWx can act as a
  * 15 fronthaul protocol converter, e.g. from eCPRI to CPRI.
